Other notes: give telogen effluvium timing from a dermatology source (AAD or DermNet), as averages: shedding usually starts about 2–4 months after the trigger and regrowth takes months. package.description:
Will tirzepatide hair loss grow back? Usually, yes. In a 2026 systematic review, 5.4% on tirzepatide reported hair loss vs 0.9% on placebo. It's linked to rapid weight loss; so far, no human studies show a direct effect of tirzepatide on follicles. Fullness tends to return within about 6 to 9 months.

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you, and don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.

Sources:
1. Eli Lilly, Zepbound prescribing information (revised Aug 2026): https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=487cd7e7-434c-4925-99fa-aa80b1cc776b
2. Gupta AK et al., Science Progress (2026): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41998799/
3. American Academy of Dermatology, Do you have hair loss or hair shedding? (2024): https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/insider/shedding
4. DermNet, Telogen effluvium (2019): https://dermnetnz.org/topics/telogen-effluvium

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: In twenty twenty-six, Gupta and colleagues published a systematic review on GLP-1 medicines and hair loss in the journal Science Progress. It reported figures for tirzepatide compared with placebo.

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Here's the headline number. Hair loss was reported in five point four percent of people on tirzepatide.

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: On placebo, it was zero point nine percent.

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: In people, that's one hundred nineteen out of two thousand one hundred eighty-three on tirzepatide, versus twenty-two out of two thousand two hundred twenty-one on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete group sizes behind the percentages

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Put simply, a bit more than one in twenty people on tirzepatide reported it, compared with just under one in a hundred on placebo.

visual.stock_query: row of twenty people, one highlighted

scenes.retention_device: Puts the numbers in human terms

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So it's real, and it's clearly above placebo. But flip it around: roughly nineteen out of twenty people on tirzepatide in those trials didn't report hair loss at all.

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The official prescribing information tells a similar story. In tirzepatide's weight-loss trials, hair loss was reported in about four to five percent of people, depending on dose, versus about one percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide label: hair loss vs 1% placebo

scenes.retention_device: A second source backs up the first

scenes.section: How Common Is Hair Loss on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So why would a medicine that works on appetite and blood sugar affect your hair at all? This is where it gets interesting.

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?

scenes.retention_device: Chapter named after the search question

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Your hair doesn't grow nonstop. Each follicle cycles through a long growing phase, a short transition, and a resting phase. Then the old hair falls out and a new one starts.
scenes.retention_device: Simple explainer with a visual loop

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: At any moment, most of your hairs are in the growing phase. Only a small share are resting.
scenes.retention_device: Sets up the shift that comes next

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: That's why losing about fifty to one hundred hairs a day is normal, according to the American Academy of Dermatology.

visual.stat_label: Hairs shed per day, normal range

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: But a big shock to the body can push many follicles into the resting phase at the same time. A few months later, those hairs let go together.

visual.stock_query: many follicles switching to sleep mode

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Doctors call this telogen effluvium. Telogen is the resting phase. Effluvium means outflow.

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The American Academy of Dermatology lists common triggers, including a high fever, giving birth, surgery, a lot of stress, and losing twenty pounds or more.

visual.stock_query: icons for fever, baby, stress, scale

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Notice that last one. Weight loss is on the list by itself, with no mention of how it happened.

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: And tirzepatide can lead to a lot of weight loss. In the SURMOUNT one trial, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, lost about twenty-one percent of their body weight on average at the highest dose, over seventy-two weeks.

visual.stat_label: SURMOUNT-1: average weight loss, top dose, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Connects the trigger to tirzepatide with a concrete number

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: On placebo, it was about three percent. That's a big change for the body to adjust to, even when it's a healthy one.

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So is the drug attacking your hair follicles? So far, no human studies show a direct effect of tirzepatide on follicles. The shedding is linked to rapid weight loss.

visual.fact: No human studies show a direct follicle effect
visual.stock_query: calm neutral mascot with myth card

scenes.section: Why Does Hair Shed on Tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: That's an honest 'so far'. The research is still young. But if this is telogen effluvium, there's genuinely good news hiding in the timing.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?
scenes.narration: With telogen effluvium, shedding usually doesn't begin right away. The American Academy of Dermatology says most people notice it a few months after the trigger. DermNet, a dermatology reference, puts it at around two to four months.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?
scenes.narration: That delay is why it feels so random. By the time Priya noticed her hairbrush, the changes in her body had started months earlier. It can feel like it came out of nowhere. Usually, it didn't.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?
scenes.narration: Now the good part. As the body readjusts, the extra shedding tends to stop. The Academy says that within about six to nine months, hair tends to regain its normal fullness.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?
scenes.narration: Why does regrowth usually happen? Because in telogen effluvium, the follicle isn't destroyed. It's resting, and it can start a new growing phase.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?
scenes.narration: One twist with tirzepatide: weight loss can carry on for many months, so the trigger isn't always a single moment like a fever or an operation.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?
scenes.narration: DermNet, a dermatology reference, notes that in some people the extra shedding carries on for long periods, sometimes years. So if heavy shedding goes on past about six months, it's worth getting checked rather than waiting it out.

scenes.section: When Does Shedding Start and Stop?

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: Let's be clear up front: nothing makes this kind of shedding stop overnight. But a few steps can support you while your hair cycle resets.

visual.stock_query: gentle reset button on hair cycle

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: First, be gentle. A wide-tooth comb, looser hairstyles, and less heat won't stop shedding, but they can avoid extra breakage on top of it. That's our practical tip, not a trial result.

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: Second, protein. Your appetite can drop a lot on tirzepatide, and it's easy to under-eat without noticing. Building each meal around a protein source is one of the most useful habits on this medicine, for your muscles and your whole body. If you have kidney disease, ask your clinician how much protein is right for you.

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: Third, that blood test I promised. The NHS lists iron deficiency among the causes of temporary hair loss. So it's reasonable to ask your clinician whether checking your iron levels makes sense for you.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the blood-test open loop

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: Fourth, be careful with hair supplements. Biotin, a popular one, can interfere with some lab test results, according to the FDA. So tell your clinician about anything you take.

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: Fifth, talk to your prescriber instead of changing anything yourself. They can look at your overall progress, how you're eating, and anything else going on. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.

scenes.section: What Helps Hair Recover?
scenes.narration: Picture Priya again. She mentions the shedding at her next appointment, gets her iron checked, and starts a protein-first breakfast. Months later, she spots short new hairs along her parting.

visual.stock_query: woman smiling at mirror, new hairs

scenes.retention_device: Emotional payoff of the hypothetical thread

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe, so it passes. The fixes below are minor and optional. I checked every key number against its source:
- **Zepbound label (revised 28 Aug 2026):** 5%, 4% and 5% by dose vs 1% placebo, 7.1% of women vs 0.5% of men, and hair loss "associated with weight reduction".
- **AAD:** 50–100 hairs a day is normal, the trigger list includes losing 20 pounds or more, shedding shows "a few months" after the trigger, and fullness returns in 6–9 months.
- **DermNet:** shedding starts 2–4 months after the trigger, the chronic form can last "sometimes for years", thinning is diffuse rather than patchy, and follicles stay intact (non-scarring).
- **NHS (reviewed 24 Jan 2024):** iron deficiency is listed among causes of temporary hair loss, and the page says to see a GP if you're worried. The script correctly labels sudden loss, patches, clumps and itch/burn as our own rule of thumb.
- **FDA:** biotin can interfere with certain lab tests generally, not just troponin.
- **SURMOUNT-1:** about 21% at 15 mg vs about 3% on placebo at 72 weeks, and the population is stated correctly.
- **Gupta 2026:** the review exists in Sci Prog 2026 (PMID 41998799). The 5.4% vs 0.9% figures and the "no human study shows a direct follicle effect" point are backed by a secondary report of the review. The 119/2,183 and 22/2,221 counts come from the craft notes; I couldn't open the paywalled full text to confirm them.
- **Wegovy 2.4 mg:** about 3% vs 1% placebo, confirmed through secondary reports of the label (the label PDF wouldn't parse).

Safety lines are all in place: the prescriber line and don't-stop line in s07 and s71, the kidney caveat on protein, a referral to a clinician rather than iron supplements, the biotin caution, and the Priya scenario is clearly hypothetical. The hook delivers on the title. One gap: the FDA approved a 7.2 mg Wegovy dose in March 2026, so the semaglutide comparison should say it covers only the 2.4 mg dose, and the S5 citation year is out of date.

issues.claim: In semaglutide's weight-loss trials in adults, at the two point four milligram dose, hair loss was reported in about three percent of people
issues.problem: The 2.4 mg figure is correct, but the FDA approved a higher 7.2 mg Wegovy dose in March 2026. In a chapter answering 'worse than semaglutide?', the script should say the comparison covers only the 2.4 mg dose. The S5 citation also gives 2025, which is out of date.
issues.fix: Add to the end of the s40 narration: "That's the two point four milligram dose. A higher semaglutide dose is now approved too, and it's not part of this comparison." In S5, change year to "2026" and the title to "WEGOVY (semaglutide) injection: Full Prescribing Information (current 2026 revision)". Check the exact revision date on DailyMed before publishing.

issues.claim: That's why losing about fifty to one hundred hairs a day is normal, according to the American Academy of Dermatology.
issues.problem: "That's why" makes the growth/rest split sound like AAD's explanation for the 50–100 figure. AAD only states the normal range.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "And shedding some hair every day is normal. The American Academy of Dermatology says fifty to one hundred hairs a day is typical."

issues.claim: For men, it was zero point five percent. … changes in hair may simply get noticed and reported more often by women.
issues.problem: The label also shows the same gap on placebo (1.3% of women vs 0% of men). That fact supports the reporting explanation and gives the women stat its comparator for muted viewers, but the script leaves it out.
issues.fix: Add a sentence after s47: "Even on placebo, women reported it more often: one point three percent, versus zero percent of men." Use on-screen text "Placebo: women 1.3%, men 0%".

issues.claim: Building each meal around a protein source is one of the most useful habits on this medicine

thumbnail.reasoning:
Candidate #0 is the format the growth playbook explicitly favors (before-after state-change, 3.8–5.0% CTR) and carries the right hedge word 'usually,' but the execution is flawed: the headline is split across a red 'HAIR' badge and the fragment 'UALLY GROWS BACK,' which does not cleanly parse to 'USUALLY GROWS BACK' at a glance, especially at phone size. A viewer skimming the feed is likely to read only 'GROWS BACK' or a garbled fragment, which either confuses them or strips the hedge and implies an absolute claim the video doesn't make — a legibility and accuracy risk, so it fails the ≥7 legibility bar needed to be eligible.

Candidate #1 is perfectly legible (clean 5.4% vs 0.9% placebo stat) but answers 'how common is this?' rather than the title's actual question ('will it grow back?'), so it has a weaker curiosity match to this specific title, and the worried/sweating mascot face brushes against the craft note to avoid scared or sweating characters. Big-number thumbnails are also a documented mid-tier performer on this channel (2.8–4.5%) versus before-after's 3.8–5.0%.

Candidate #2 ('WHY WOMEN MORE?') is cleanly legible at every size, has one strong labelled focal character with high contrast against a bold purple background, and opens a real curiosity gap tied to a genuine, evidence-backed finding in the video (7.1% women vs 0.5% men). It doesn't literally restate the title (satisfying the no-repeat rule) and isn't sensational — it poses a fact-based question the video actually answers. Its main soft issue is that it leads with a different sub-question than the title's headline question, but since the video does cover this finding, it's not misleading, just a different valid hook. Given #0 fails on legibility and #1 is weaker on both title-match and mascot tone, #2 is the strongest eligible choice for CTR while staying honest and clear.

issues.claim: Will tirzepatide hair loss grow back? Usually, yes. In a 2026 systematic review, 5.4% on tirzepatide reported hair loss vs 0.9% on placebo (119/2,183 vs 22/2,221). It is linked to rapid weight loss; no human studies show a direct effect on follicles. Shedding often starts a few months after the trigger, and fullness tends to return within about 6 to 9 months.
